koi_period.name: Orbital Period
koi_period.plain_description: The time it takes the candidate to complete one full orbit around its host star.
koi_period.detection_significance: Ultra-short periods (< 1 day) or extreme values can indicate contact binary stars or tidal synchronization. Genuine habitable zone planets typically have longer periods.
koi_period.planet_tendency: Moderate to long periods are typical for multi-planet systems; extreme ultra-short periods often require high scrutiny.

koi_duration.name: Transit Duration
koi_duration.plain_description: How long the star's light is partially blocked during the transit.
koi_duration.detection_significance: Transit duration is tied directly to orbital velocity and stellar density via Kepler's laws. Grazing eclipsing binaries often produce abnormally brief, V-shaped transit dips.
koi_duration.planet_tendency: Consistent, central-transit durations aligned with circular orbits favor planet status.

koi_depth.name: Transit Depth
koi_depth.plain_description: The fraction of starlight blocked by the object, measured in parts per million (1% = 10,000 ppm).
koi_depth.detection_significance: Earth blocks ~84 ppm; Jupiter blocks ~10,000 ppm (1%). Dips greater than 20,000-30,000 ppm (2-3%) usually indicate a stellar companion (eclipsing binary), not a planet.
koi_depth.planet_tendency: Shallow to moderate depths (< 10,000 ppm) strongly favor exoplanets. Extremely deep dips (> 20,000 ppm) signal impostors.

koi_prad.name: Planetary Radius
koi_prad.plain_description: The inferred size of the object relative to Earth (Earth = 1.0 R⊕, Neptune = ~3.9 R⊕, Jupiter = ~11.2 R⊕).
koi_prad.detection_significance: Objects larger than ~20 to 30 Earth radii are astrophysically too large to be planets—they are almost certainly low-mass stars or brown dwarfs.
koi_prad.planet_tendency: Sizes between 0.5 and 15 R⊕ strongly favor exoplanets. Values > 25 R⊕ are almost always false positives.

koi_teq.name: Equilibrium Temperature
koi_teq.plain_description: Estimated atmospheric temperature of the planet assuming uniform heat distribution (Earth is ~255 K without greenhouse effect).
koi_teq.detection_significance: Helps distinguish hot Jupiters from temperate worlds. Outlier temperatures point to extreme proximity or stellar radiation.
koi_teq.planet_tendency: Physical planetary atmospheres generally peak below 3,000 K.

koi_insol.name: Insolation Flux
koi_insol.plain_description: The amount of stellar radiation hitting the planet compared to Earth (Earth = 1.0 S⊕).
koi_insol.detection_significance: Measures irradiance. Extremely high insolation (> 10,000 S⊕) indicates an object grazing the stellar surface.
koi_insol.planet_tendency: Earth-like to Jupiter-like fluxes favor normal exoplanetary environments.

koi_model_snr.name: Signal-to-Noise Ratio
koi_model_snr.plain_description: The strength of the transit signal compared to background detector and stellar noise.
koi_model_snr.detection_significance: Low SNR (< 7.1) candidates are frequently spurious noise spikes or statistical fluctuations. High SNR indicates a clear, reliable transit signal.
koi_model_snr.planet_tendency: Solid SNR (> 15-20) indicates real astrophysical signals, though high SNR can also be caused by bright eclipsing binaries.

koi_impact.name: Impact Parameter (b)
koi_impact.plain_description: The projected distance from the center of the stellar disk to the transit chord (0.0 = dead center, 1.0 = edge of star).
koi_impact.detection_significance: Values > 1.0 indicate a grazing transit where only a fraction of the transiting body clips the stellar disk. Grazing eclipsing binaries mimic planetary dips.
koi_impact.planet_tendency: Values between 0.0 and 0.85 are typical for central planetary transits. Values >= 1.0 strongly correlate with false positives.

koi_steff.name: Stellar Effective Temperature
koi_steff.plain_description: The surface temperature of the host star (our Sun is ~5,778 K; red dwarfs are ~3,000-4,000 K).
koi_steff.detection_significance: Characterizes the stellar host type (M, K, G, F, A dwarf). Proper host parameters are critical to derive accurate planetary properties.
koi_steff.planet_tendency: Normal main-sequence stars (4,000 - 6,500 K) host the majority of confirmed Kepler worlds.

koi_slogg.name: Stellar Surface Gravity (log g)
koi_slogg.plain_description: The gravitational acceleration at the star's surface on a logarithmic scale (Sun = 4.44).
koi_slogg.detection_significance: Main-sequence dwarf stars have log g around 4.0 to 4.6. Lower values (< 3.8) indicate giant or subgiant stars, which rarely show clean planetary transits.
koi_slogg.planet_tendency: Values >= 4.1 indicate stable dwarf stars with well-understood planetary transit geometry.

koi_srad.name: Stellar Radius
koi_srad.plain_description: The radius of the host star compared to our Sun (Sun = 1.0 R⊙).
koi_srad.detection_significance: Because transit depth measures (R_planet / R_star)², if the star is actually a giant star (e.g. 10 R⊙), what looked like an Earth-sized planet is actually a Jupiter or a star.
koi_srad.planet_tendency: Compact dwarf stars (0.7 – 1.4 R⊙) yield the cleanest, highest-confidence planet confirmations.
